posts.title: Snapshot isolation still allows write skew
posts.body:
Snapshot isolation stops dirty reads and lost updates, but two transactions can read the same snapshot and write disjoint rows that together break an invariant.
- Classic case: two doctors both check that another is on call, then both go off call.
- Fixes: `SELECT FOR UPDATE` on a shared row, materialized conflicts, or serializable isolation (SSI).
👉 Ask which invariant spans more than one row before you pick an isolation level.

posts.title: Write amplification is the real LSM cost
posts.body:
LSM trees are fast at writes because they append and compact later. The price is that one logical write is rewritten many times.
- Leveled compaction: lower read and space amplification, higher write amplification.
- Size-tiered: cheaper writes, more files to read and more space used.
👉 Pick the compaction strategy from your read-to-write ratio, not from benchmarks.

posts.title: Exactly-once is an end-to-end property
posts.body:
Idempotent producers and transactions give exactly-once inside Kafka. They do not cover the side effect you run in your consumer.
- Commit the offset and the state change in the same database transaction.
- Or make the handler idempotent with a dedupe key.
👉 If the sink is not transactional, the guarantee is at-least-once plus idempotency.

posts.title: Why Raft only commits entries from the current term
posts.body:
A leader must not count replicas for entries from earlier terms when deciding commit. A later leader can overwrite them.
- Commit happens only when an entry from the current term is replicated to a majority.
- Earlier entries then commit indirectly.
👉 This rule is the one most reimplementations get wrong.

posts.title: Fan-out at celebrity scale
posts.body:
Pushing one post to 50M followers on write blows up the write path. Pulling on read blows up latency. Real systems do both, split by follower count.
👉 Swipe for the hybrid design.

slides.title: The two extremes
slides.body:
- Fan-out on write: fast reads, huge write burst per celebrity post
- Fan-out on read: cheap writes, merge cost paid by every reader

slides.title: Where it breaks
slides.body: A single celebrity can produce 50M queue messages. Your queues and workers become the bottleneck, not the database.

slides.title: Hybrid by threshold
slides.body: Users under a follower threshold are pushed to follower timelines. Celebrity posts are pulled and merged at read time.
slides.code:
if followers(author) < T: push(post, followers)
else: mark_celebrity(post)  # merged at read

slides.title: Protect the merge
slides.body: Cache the celebrity timeline slices per user. Bound the merge to the last N posts so read cost stays flat.

slides.title: Takeaway
slides.body: **Pick the write or read path per segment.** One global strategy fails at one end of the distribution.

posts.title: Consistent hashing with bounded loads
posts.body:
Plain consistent hashing gives balanced keys on average, but a hot key or uneven node still overloads one node.
- Cap each node at a load factor, such as 1.25 times the mean.
- A key that finds its node full moves to the next node on the ring.
👉 Lets you smooth load without losing most of the cache locality.

posts.title: Double-checked locking is only right with volatile
posts.body:
Lazy singletons with double-checked locking look safe. Without a volatile field, a thread can see a partly constructed object.
- The write to the reference can be reordered before the constructor's writes.
- `volatile` adds the happens-before edge that makes publication safe.
👉 Or use the initialization-on-demand holder idiom and skip the locking entirely.

posts.title: Token bucket vs sliding window: pick by burst policy
posts.body:
Both enforce a rate. They differ in what a burst looks like to the client.
- Token bucket allows bounded bursts up to bucket size.
- Sliding window log is exact but memory heavy; sliding counter approximates it.
👉 State the burst policy in the interview before the data structure.

posts.title: Observers that outlive their subscribers leak
posts.body:
A subject holding strong references to listeners keeps dead UI or service objects alive.
- Hold listeners through weak references, or require explicit unsubscribe.
- Notify over a snapshot copy so listeners can unsubscribe during dispatch.
👉 Iterating the live list while a listener removes itself is a classic ConcurrentModification bug.

posts.title: Why PagedAttention fixed KV cache fragmentation
posts.body:
Preallocating the maximum context per request wastes most of GPU memory. Paging the KV cache into fixed blocks removes that waste.
- Blocks are allocated on demand and need not be contiguous.
- Requests that share a prefix can share blocks copy-on-write.
👉 Throughput gains come from packing more concurrent requests, not from faster math.

posts.title: Speculative decoding keeps the output distribution exact
posts.body:
A small draft model proposes several tokens. The large model verifies them in one forward pass.
- Accepted tokens use rejection sampling, so the distribution matches the large model.
- Speedup depends on the acceptance rate, not on the draft model's raw quality alone.
👉 A draft that is cheap and well aligned beats a bigger draft.

posts.title: Measure retrieval before you touch the prompt
posts.body:
Most RAG failures are retrieval failures that look like generation failures.
- Build a labelled set of queries with gold chunks.
- Track recall@k and MRR for retrieval separately from answer quality.
👉 Add a reranker only after recall@k is already high.

posts.title: Patch size sets the compute budget of a ViT
posts.body:
Self-attention cost grows with the square of the token count. Halving the patch side quadruples the tokens and roughly multiplies attention cost by 16.
- Smaller patches keep fine detail but explode the sequence length.
- Higher resolution at a fixed patch size costs the same way.
👉 Choose patch size from the smallest object you must detect, then budget resolution.

posts.title: Reliability is about faults you expect
posts.body:
A reliable system keeps working correctly when things go wrong, even when faults are common.
- Faults are inevitable: hardware, software bugs, and human error.
- Design so that faults are contained and recovery is routine.
👉 Practice the failure before the incident does.

posts.title: Regression to the mean fools good managers
posts.body:
Extreme results tend to be followed by less extreme ones, even with no intervention.
- Praise after a great quarter often precedes a weaker one.
- Punishment after a bad one often precedes improvement.
👉 Judge a change by the trend across many periods, not by the last one.
